series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm: swap: move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the insertion of a folio into the LRU (Least Recently Used) list out of the swap cache allocator. The swap cache allocator is used by zswap writeback to allocate a folio that can be freed directly once writeback completes, without being on the LRU. This change does not introduce any functional changes and only modifies the internal implementation details of the swap cache allocator.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm: swap: drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of drop-behind swap cache folios by freeing them immediately after writeback completion, rather than leaving them for reclaim to find later. This is done by adding two new functions: `swap_writeback_dropbehind_folio` and `swap_dropbehind_free_one_folio`, which are called when a synchronous-IO swap completes or an asynchronous block device completes writeback. The patch also updates the `remove_mapping` function to take additional parameters for tracking reclaim status and target memory cgroup. This change is necessary because synchronous-IO swaps can complete in the calling context, allowing the folio to be freed immediately, while asynchronous block devices require deferring the work to a workqueue that runs after writeback completion.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm: zswap: drop cold writeback folios via swap dropbehind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in zswap by dropping cold writeback folios via the swap dropbehind mechanism, reducing unnecessary reclaim scans and keeping cold memory resident for shorter periods.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch reintroduces a fixup mechanism to handle a specific scenario where a dio read operation sees a dirty destination page, but by the time it finishes reading, the page is clean due to btrfs writing it back. The fixup ensures that the dio read re-dirties the folio to prevent data corruption. This patch addresses an issue that was previously thought to be resolved with advances in preventing such re-dirtying, and reintroduces a mechanism that was first introduced in 2008.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] btrfs: use GFP_NOWAIT for tree block readahead

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] btrfs: use GFP_NOWAIT for tree block readahead

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the btrfs readahead mechanism to use GFP_NOWAIT instead of the default GFP_KERNEL allocation flag. This change is intended to prevent the readahead from blocking in direct reclaim, which can cause stalls and lock contention. The approach taken is to mark the extent buffer preallocation as supporting nowait allocation, allowing the system to fail the readahead if necessary rather than waiting for memory to become available.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] btrfs: enable unlocked NOFAIL retry for eb allocations

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] btrfs: enable unlocked NOFAIL retry for eb allocations

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch enables unlocked NOFAIL retry for extent buffer (eb) allocations in the Btrfs file system. It introduces a new struct, btrfs_eb_prealloc, to carry allocation information and signals when preallocation is required. If the allocation fails, it returns EAGAIN and allows the caller to retry with the eb, block device, and folios wired through in the prealloc struct. This approach aims to reduce reclaim stalls by allowing allocations that fail due to lack of memory to be retried without holding locks. However, two GFP_NOFS allocations remain under lock and cannot be preallocated.

The existing allocation pathways are refactored to use this new structure without any functional changes. Empty prealloc structs are wired in from callers, and several files have been modified as a result.

version_history.subject: [PATCH v2 0/4] allocate extent_buffer GFP_NOFAIL with unlocked retry

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in the Btrfs file system where allocations of extent_buffers are often made while holding btree locks, leading to contention and stalls. The patches introduce a mechanism to allocate these buffers with GFP_NOWAIT, then retry with GFP_NOFS | GFP_NOFAIL if necessary without holding any locks. This approach is analogous to how extent_buffers are read, which requires dropping locks. Although the series does not completely eliminate lock-holding allocations, it significantly reduces contention and stalls.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 01/21] iomap: split iomap_iter() logic into iomap_iter_next()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the iomap_iter() logic into a new helper function called iomap_iter_next(). The purpose of this change is to prepare for an upcoming modification to use an in-iterator model, where the ->iomap_next() callback will be able to directly call the iomap_iter_next() function. This allows for more flexibility and simplification of code. Additionally, two new macros are introduced to generate boilerplate wrapper functions for ->iomap_next(). The patch does not introduce any functional changes, but rather a code-level refactoring.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/21] iomap: decouple simple direct I/O reads from iomap_dio_rw
series_items.patch_summary: This patch decouples simple direct I/O reads from the iomap_dio_rw function to improve performance by allowing file systems to call into a new simple path explicitly, which can be inlined and optimized by the compiler. This change is necessary because the current implementation assumes that the iterator must be advanced at the end, but the direct I/O read fast path tries to avoid this. By splitting the simple path from iomap_dio_rw, file systems are required to only call the simple path for cases they can handle, and various checks for incompatible features can be dropped.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series converts the iomap code to use an iterator model, replacing the current begin/end pair of callbacks with a single next callback. This change allows for improved performance by enabling inlining and devirtualization of the iteration loop, as well as providing more flexibility for future callers to express custom logic in the IO path. The patches are broken down into 21 steps, including refactoring existing code, adding the new next callback, converting each filesystem, removing legacy paths, and updating documentation.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about the iomap_iter() logic, moved it out into an inlined helper function called iomap_iter_next(), and provided macros to generate boilerplate ->iomap_next() wrapper functions. No functional change intended.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged that the pending iomap_iter_next conversion creates performance issues for the new simple direct I/O read fast path, agreed to split the simple path from iomap_dio_rw and require file systems to call into it explicitly, and pass only a ->begin callback. This will allow dropping various checks for incompatible features while creating a requirement for the file system to only call the simple path for cases that it can handle.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed a concern about GFP_KERNEL allocation in non-blocking iocbs, agreed to switch to GFP_NOWAIT allocation instead.

review_comments.author: Joanne Koong (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the fallback path for filesystems that don't provide an ->iomap_next() callback, explaining that iomap_iter() will fall back to the ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end() path. The author's response suggests no immediate fix or revision needed.
review_comments.raw_body:
Have one ->iomap_next() callback instead of ->iomap_begin() and
->iomap_end(). ->iomap_next() finishes the previous mapping if needed,
and produces the next mapping.

Collapsing to a single callback lets a performance-critical caller
inline its iteration loop and pass its ->iomap_next() function as a
compile-time constant, so the compiler can devirtualize that callback
into a direct call instead of an indirect call through a function
pointer.

iomap_iter() uses ->iomap_next() when the filesystem provides that
callback and otherwise falls back to the ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end()
path, so filesystems can be converted one at a time.

Suggested-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Suggested-by: Matthew Wilcox (Oracle) <willy@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>
---
 fs/iomap/iter.c       | 8 ++++++--
 include/linux/iomap.h | 9 +++++++++
 2 files changed, 15 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

diff --git a/fs/iomap/iter.c b/fs/iomap/iter.c
index 66ccb87441ab..e05574602946 100644
--- a/fs/iomap/iter.c
+++ b/fs/iomap/iter.c
@@ -107,8 +107,12 @@ int iomap_iter(struct iomap_iter *iter, const struct iomap_ops *ops)
 
 	trace_iomap_iter(iter, ops, _RET_IP_);
 
-	ret = iomap_iter_next(iter, &iter->iomap, &iter->srcmap,
-			ops->iomap_begin, ops->iomap_end);
+	if (ops->iomap_next)
+		ret = ops->iomap_next(iter, &iter->iomap, &iter->srcmap);
+	else
+		ret = iomap_iter_next(iter, &iter->iomap, &iter->srcmap,
+				ops->iomap_begin, ops->iomap_end);
+
 	iter->status = 0;
 	if (ret > 0)
 		iomap_iter_done(iter);
diff --git a/include/linux/iomap.h b/include/linux/iomap.h
index 80832edc7ec2..d203d9fe0f89 100644
--- a/include/linux/iomap.h
+++ b/include/linux/iomap.h
@@ -231,9 +231,18 @@ typedef int (*iomap_iter_begin_fn)(struct inode *inode, loff_t pos,
 typedef int (*iomap_iter_end_fn)(struct inode *inode, loff_t pos, loff_t length,
 		ssize_t written, unsigned flags, struct iomap *iomap);
 
+/*
+ * Produce the next mapping (finishing the previous one if needed).
+ * Return 1 to continue iterating, 0 if the range is fully consumed, or a
+ * negative error on failure.
+ */
+typedef int (*iomap_iter_next_fn)(const struct iomap_iter *iter,
+		struct iomap *iomap, struct iomap *srcmap);
+
 struct iomap_ops {
 	iomap_iter_begin_fn iomap_begin;
 	iomap_iter_end_fn iomap_end;
+	iomap_iter_next_fn iomap_next;
 };
 
 /**

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/4] mm: page_alloc: __GFP_FS lockdep annotation for direct compaction
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds lockdep annotations to the direct compaction function in the Linux kernel's page allocation code, specifically for __GFP_FS passing errors. This is done to prevent potential issues when compaction enters filesystem paths and to future-proof against unexpected behavior. The annotation is similar to one already present in direct reclaim code, which is often used in conjunction with compaction.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/4] mm: compaction: support non-movable compaction for pageblock requests
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the compaction algorithm in Linux by allowing non-movable direct compaction for pageblock requests, which is particularly useful in defrag_mode where whole blocks are produced and type mixing is not an issue.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Understood and agreed that the CMA interaction makes sense in this context. Provided a Reviewed-by tag.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Jul 22, 2026 at 10:56:45AM -0400, Johannes Weiner wrote:
> While trying to fix a reclaim storm in defrag_mode, I noticed that
> non-movable direct compaction is extremely inefficient.
> 
> When searching for space to evacuate, compaction only allows blocks of
> the same type as the incoming request. This is to prevent migratetype
> pollution, where a small non-movable request frees space in a movable
> block and provokes the allocator to fall back and pollute it.
> 
> This protection is reasonable on one hand, but the downside is that it
> makes non-movable direct compaction nearly useless: if we get the type
> annotations right, by definition there aren't any movable pages inside
> the non-movable blocks it is allowed to scan.
> 
> With defrag_mode, the goal is the production of whole blocks, which
> are essentially type neutral: __rmqueue_claim() will convert them
> wholesale on alloc. This makes type mixing and pollution a non-issue.
> 
> Fix the pollution gates to take the requested order into account, and
> allow whole-block requests to scan blocks of other types.
> 
> The only exception is CMA blocks. That type is sticky and these blocks
> cannot be claimed to other types. Continue to be strict with them, and
> allow only explicit ALLOC_CMA requests and kcompactd to evacuate them.
> 
> Reviewed-by: Vlastimil Babka (SUSE) <vbabka@kernel.org>
> Signed-off-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>

The CMA interaction took a second to grok but this makes sense.

Reviewed-by: Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net>

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] mm: page_alloc: move capture_control to the page allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the capture control from compaction's live compact control to the page allocator, allowing it to maintain its own copies of relevant information such as zone, migratetype, and allocation order. This change is necessary because defrag_mode promotes sub-block allocations to pageblock-order compaction, which can cause the allocation request order and compaction target order to differ. The patch also updates various functions in mm/compaction.c to pass the capture control through instead of a bare struct page pointer. No functional changes are introduced by this patch.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] mm: page_alloc: fix non-movable reclaim storm in defrag_mode
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a 'reclaim storm' issue in the Linux kernel's page allocation system, specifically in defrag_mode. The problem occurs when non-movable requests spin in reclaim, causing excessive swapping and pressure spikes on certain workloads. To fix this, the patch sends non-movable requests into pageblock reclaim/compaction, allowing them to help move pages along and meet the ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT bar. This approach is a temporary solution until a more comprehensive fix can be implemented to address scaling and concurrency limitations in compaction.

review_comments.summary:
The author acknowledged that the patch is an optimization for requests limited by block contiguity, rather than capacity, and noted redundancy between allocator and reclaim. They assumed there's no significant difference in calling compaction first or reclaim first, but haven't tested it.

review_comments.raw_body:
My understanding is that this is just an optimization for requests
that are more likely shape-limited (block contiguity) rather than
capacity-limited (free order-0). In that case we do a quick async
compaction attempt first and skip a potentially unnecessary but still
disruptive reclaim invocation.

allocator and reclaim: direct reclaim also has that early bailout
condition on compaction_ready() for costly orders.

is not much difference from which we call first - although I have not
tested it.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses reclaim storms in defrag_mode by allowing non-movable requests to participate in pageblock production during direct reclaim and compaction, which helps prevent pressure spikes and swap storms. The patches make adjustments to the allocator and compaction code to enable this behavior, including changes to capture control and migration source scan restrictions. The approach taken is to modify the slowpath of the allocator to invoke direct reclaim and compaction with pageblock_order when non-movable requests are involved. This has been tested in production against affected workloads for several weeks and restores OOM kill rates to baseline levels.
